Seminar Title:

Measuring the Effect of Artificial Intelligence Marketing Activities on Purchase Intention and Resistance Intention: A Study of the E-commerce Industry

Abstract:

The quick adoption of Artificial Intelligence has brought revolution into marketing by allowing firms to deliver personalized, interactive, and data-driven consumer experiences. In spite of its increasing application, the current knowledge is dispersed, where there is no adequate understanding about Artificial Intelligence Marketing as an organizational capability, and a lack of knowledge about both its positive and negative impact on consumer behavior at once. This research work attempts to fill the gap by employing sequential mixed-method research approach and addressing three inter-related research objectives. Specifically, the study conducted systematic literature review of AIM following SPAR-4-SLR protocol to analyze the AIM literature using Antecedents-Decisions-Outcomes and Theories-Context-Methods frameworks. Secondly, the study constructed and validated the Artificial Intelligence Marketing Activities scale based on qualitative and quantitative techniques and proved the multidimensionality of the concept through which it comprises of six dimensions of affinity, customization, information, interaction, problem-solving ability, and responsiveness. Finally, a conceptual model based on the S-O-R framework, Psychological Ownership Theory, and Privacy Calculus Theory was empirically tested to investigate dual impact of AIMA on consumer behavior in the Indian e-commerce environment. As a result, it is found that AIMA creates value by empowering consumers and generating their psychological ownership and purchase intentions, while it also generates vigilance through their privacy concern, human identity threat, and resistance intentions. Thus, the findings confirm the existence of the AI Marketing Paradox. The theoretical contributions include consolidation of the AIM literature, construction and validation of multidimensional AIMA scale, and development of a dual path model explaining the enabling and constraining effect of AIMA.
